statement: Lecture 10 agenda: a word dictionary without using any database, and a superfast key-value store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda - Word dictionary without using any DB - Superfast KV store

statement: Problem: build a word dictionary with no traditional database; be creative.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Word Dictionary without any DB ... No traditional database Be creative

statement: The dictionary must be scalable in both storage and API servers, and portable; high response time is acceptable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: scalable [ Storage & API servers ] portable Response time can be high

statement: Words and meanings are updated weekly through a changelog, not continuously.
detail: Board spells 'updakd' [sic, updated].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: words and Meanings updakd weekly through a changelog

statement: A lookup is always a single word; the dictionary is 1 TB big and has 170,000 words.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: lookup is always a singular word - dictionary is 1TB big & has 170,000 words

statement: The dictionary file must not contain repeated entries for the same word.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: no repetitive entries

statement: Brainstorm the design along four axes: storage, querying, portability and seamless updates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Brainstorm storage, querying, portability, seamless updates

statement: A single JSON file is rejected (struck out); the dictionary is stored as a plain text file of word, meaning lines.
detail: JSON is scribbled over in pink at 00:06:45-00:08:15; audio: the whole JSON must be read and deserialized to look up one word.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Text file JSON file apple , a fruit amazon, a rainforest

statement: Requirements raised in discussion: searchable via key, very read heavy, each update should not be costly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: "searchable" via key read heavy (very) each update should not be costly

statement: Sorting the file by key enables efficient search.
detail: Replaces the earlier 'Sort??'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: sort by key ⟶ efficient search

statement: Splitting the dictionary into multiple files was raised and erased: it breaks portability.
detail: Written at 00:14:00, erased by 00:20:30 when the teacher insists on one file for portability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: can we have multiple files??

statement: Naive lookup is a linear scan of the whole 1 TB file per request.
detail: Shown by a red arrow down the file box; only '1TB' is written.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1TB

statement: To make reads fast, build an index.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: "Indexing"

statement: The index stores each word with the byte offset of its line in the data file.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: apple, o1 amazon, o2 book, o3

statement: Index size estimate: 170,000 words x (4.3 avg word length + 4-byte offset + 2 for comma and newline) = 10.3 x 170,000 B = 1,751,000 B ≈ 1.751 MB.
detail: The meaning of each term (avg word length, offset, comma + newline) comes from the audio.
speaker: teacher

statement: The index (about 1.75 MB) fits easily in memory.
detail: Inference from the circled result; stated in audio.
speaker: teacher

statement: The index and data live in two files, index.dict and data.dict.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: index.dict data.dict

statement: For portability, combine index and data into one file: index section then data section.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Index data Portable

statement: Option to mark where the index ends: a special line / separator.
detail: Student proposal; superseded by storing the byte offset in a header.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: special line / separator

statement: Option: pre-allocate a fixed size (e.g. 2 MB) for the index section.
detail: Student proposal; in audio the teacher calls it a nice hack that wastes a little space and moves on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: pre-allocate / Fixed size 2MB

statement: Add a header at the start of the file storing the byte offset of the data section.
detail: Board spells 'byk' [sic, byte].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: header byk offset of data

statement: Header fields: magic name OUR_DICT (8 B), version (4 B), index size (4 B) - a fixed 16-byte header.
detail: 'index size' replaced an earlier 'St offset of data' line. 8B is written like 'gB'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: header → OUR_DICT - 8B → Version - 4B → index size - 4B 16B

statement: A format can name itself with magic bytes, e.g. a made-up 'AOBB' database format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: AOBB

statement: Every file format has an encoder and a decoder (examples on board: parquet, JSON).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: parquet JSON Encoder & Decoder

statement: Serving setup: user sends GET /word to a load balancer in front of API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: L B API Servers GET /word

statement: Keeping a copy of the file on every API server makes updates tedious, risks inconsistency, and above all costs too much.
detail: Board spellings 'updak' [update], 'inconsiknoy' [inconsistency].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: updak tedious inconsiknoy. COST !!

statement: Keep the single file in central storage (S3) and do pointed reads on it.
detail: 'Poinkd' [sic, Pointed]; end cut off at page edge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3 Poinkd Rea[d]

statement: What is needed is network attached storage with file-system semantics: random reads of n bytes at an offset of a file.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Network attachd Storage + File System Semantics (Random Read) ( file, off, n )

statement: HDFS or a network hard disk can replace S3 here.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: HDFS Netwok HDD

statement: Each API server knows the file path on S3, loads the index into an in-memory word → offset map, then reads entries from S3 by offset.
detail: The in-memory map is drawn as a yellow spiral in each API server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Filepath on S3 ω→o

statement: Updates arrive weekly as a changelog of changed words.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: updak: weekly apple: — ball: — zoo: —

statement: A separate server downloads the dictionary from S3 and the changelog to apply the update.
detail: Drawn only (arrow from S3 down to a server holding two files).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: [drawing only]

statement: Appending changes at the end of the dictionary was proposed.
detail: Rejected in audio: the file would keep growing and contain duplicate entries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: append at end

statement: Overwriting an entry in place on disk with a longer value overwrites the following bytes, corrupting the next entry.
detail: Shown by writing 'a round fruit' over 'a fruit' so it runs into 'ball, a round obj'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: apple, a round fruit apple, a fruit ball, a round obj

statement: Instead, write a new file, and keep it sorted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: new file ↳ Sorted

statement: Merge walkthrough: sorted dictionary a..h and sorted changelog c'', e', f'' merge with two pointers into a new dictionary that takes the changelog value where keys match.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Dictionary Changelog c - c'' e - e' f - f'' New dic a - a' ... c - c'' ... f - f''

statement: The merged file is uploaded back to S3.
detail: Drawn only: yellow curve from the new file to the S3 cloud.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: [drawing only]

statement: Upload the new dictionary to a new S3 path so the transfer and the transition are smooth.
detail: 'tranfer' [sic, transfer].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: upload to new S3 path tranfer smooth smooth transition

statement: Uploading to the same location breaks reads: servers still hold the old index, so the old offset points into a different line of the new file and users see garbage.
detail: Prepared notes page.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: apple: 100, 1024 data.dat [new] Something random !! User sees garbage response during lookup.

statement: Note: servers have already loaded the old index built for the old dictionary data.
detail: Prepared notes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Note: Servers have already loaded the old index built for old dictionary data

statement: Transition option 1: periodic refresh (pull) of the server's index; between the S3 change and the next pull users get garbage; needs graceful termination / reload.
detail: Prepared notes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. Periodic refresh of server's index pull index.dat change on S3 garbage response Graceful Termination | Reload

statement: Transition option 2: reactive Pub/Sub - a standalone updater publishes to Redis and the API servers subscribe and reload.
detail: Prepared notes; option 3 'Parallel Setup' is listed but its content is not shown.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 2. Reactive: PubSub Redis API Standalone

statement: Version the S3 path: dict1.dict, then dict2.dict for the new dictionary.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3:// wd/ dict1.dict S3:// wd/ dict2.dict

statement: A static meta.json on S3 holds the current dictionary path; servers can poll it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: polling metafile meta.json { path: "" }

statement: A Redis Pub/Sub channel could notify servers reactively instead of polling.
detail: Drawn only (pipe below the API servers, erased by 01:42:45).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: [drawing only]

statement: Simplest: after updating meta.json, trigger a deployment via the AWS SDK; booting servers read meta.json and load the new file.
detail: Board shows only the two labels and arrows; the boot-reads-meta.json logic is from the audio.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: AWS SDK Deploy

statement: Prepared procedure: spin up a new server, download dictionary and changelog, merge in O(n) to create a new dict and index locally, upload them to S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Spinup a new server - download the dictionary locally - download the changelog - merge in O(n), create a new dict & index locally

statement: Merge is O(n) because the dictionary and the index are sorted: it is merging two sorted lists.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How is merge O(n)? Dictionary is sorted. Index is sorted Merge → Merging of two sorted lists

statement: Prepared alternative: one file per word in a folder per first character on S3; lookup builds the S3 path - but it breaks portability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Folder for each char ... But it breaks a major requirement Portability

statement: Prepared sizing: 171,476 words; entry = avg word length 4.7 + 3 (separator + newline) + 2x4; index ≈ 15.7 x 171,476 = 2,692,173.2 B ≈ 2.6 MB.
detail: Prepared notes differ from the live estimate (170,000 x 10.3 ≈ 1.75 MB); the 2x4 term and the 3 are as written.
speaker: teacher

statement: Prepared read flow: on boot the API server loads the index file into memory; per request it looks up the offset in memory, reads the entry from S3 and returns the meaning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API server on boot → loads the index file in memory → upon receiving a req → lookup in index (memory) → find offset

statement: Real-world use: multi-tiered storage - historical orders on S3, latest orders on MySQL - without losing the ability to query the data.
detail: 'lakst' [latest], 'loosing' [losing].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Multitiered Storage historical orders on S3 lakst orders on MySQL Without loosing an ability to Query the data

statement: Athena and data lakes work on the same idea.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Athena Data lake

statement: Part 2: a superfast key-value store - superfast reads, writes, deletes, with persistence.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Superfast DB KV Requirements : superfast reads, writes, deletes, persistence

statement: Magnetic disk: data lives in sectors of spinning platters; reads need head and platter movement.
detail: Drawn only: platter ellipse with one dotted sector; the mechanics are from the audio.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: [drawing only]

statement: Speed scale: memory fastest, then SSD, HDD slowest.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SSD M HDD

statement: PUT appends to an append-only file: zero seek, no big mechanical movement - the best possible on disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Append only Zero seek no big mech movement Best we can do!!

statement: PUT K1 V1, K2 V2, K3 V3, K1 V1' are appended in order; the update of K1 is a new row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: PUT K1 V1 PUT K2 V2 PUT K3 V3 PUT K1 V1'

statement: DEL is a PUT with a special value: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1)

statement: An in-memory hash table maps each key to the offset of its latest entry (K1 → O4 after the update).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in-mem K1 → O4 K3 → O3

statement: Limitation: the index (keys) must fit in RAM; the file grows huge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: amount of index fit in ram * Keys File grows huge!!!

statement: File rotation: files 001-004; one active file takes writes, older files are read only; the index stores file and offset.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 001 002 003 004 Read Only K1 → f1, O4 File Rotation

statement: Merge and compaction combines the read-only files.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Merge & Compaction

statement: Disk usage forms a sawtooth below the disk cap (e.g. 1 TB); the two tuning knobs are merge-compaction frequency and file rotation threshold.
detail: Labels cut off at the page edge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1TB 1. MC freq 2. file rot[ation] thresh[old]

statement: Append-only writes give high write throughput even on HDD ('5000x gain'); SSDs do not give a similar gain.
detail: Prepared notes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High write throughput even on HDD The SSD does not give similar gain 5000x gain

statement: Simplest design: a single file of KV pairs; PUT(K,V) appends to the file - a lightning-fast operation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Simplest design : single files of KV pairs PUT(K,V) → append to this file lightning fast operation

statement: Records need key size and value size fields because keys and values are variable length; reading until newline is not optimal.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we cannot read "until newline" ... not optimal Because key and value are variable length KSZ VSZ K V

statement: Read KSZ (4 bytes) and VSZ (4 bytes), then read KSZ bytes for the key and VSZ bytes for the value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we read KSZ (4b) VSZ(4b) & then read KSZ bytes for key VSZ bytes for value

statement: Integrity problem: the machine can crash while writing a value, leaving a partial record.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Solving integrity machine crashed while writing value

statement: Detect corrupt entries with a CRC written first; record = CRC | TS | KSZ | VSZ | K | V, where TS is a timestamp for conflicts.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Finding carroupt entries : CRC → First thing we flush CRC TS KSZ VSZ K V Timestamp for conflicts

statement: GET(k) is a pointed query: hash table lookup, disk seek, disk read - O(1) with an index.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: To get O(1) GET we Index GET(k) → pointed queries - Hash table lookup - disk seek - disk read

statement: Rotate the file every 't' bytes: the old file becomes immutable and available for reads; only one file is ACTIVE and takes writes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Rotate the file every 't' bytes ... old file is made immutable ... only one is "ACTIVE"

statement: Each in-memory index entry holds File ID, value size (entry size), value position (offset) and timestamp.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: K1 → File ID VSZ VPOS TS offset timestamp

statement: Merge & compact all immutable files, skipping stale and deleted entries; offsets change, so update the index atomically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all immutable files are merged & compacted stale entries skipped deleted entries skipped update index atomically!

statement: Limitation: keys must fit in memory. Strengths: O(1) reads, writes, deletes; high throughput, low latency; I/O saturation; easy backups.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Keys musl fil in memory O(1) reads, writes, deletes High throughput, low latency I/O saturation Eazy Backups

statement: The design is Bitcask.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What we just designed is Bitcask

statement: Bitcask is used by Uber in production as the backend of Riak; each Riak node runs a Bitcask instance behind a proxy.
detail: Prepared notes; 'instance' cut off by tiles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: used by uber in production as Backend for Riak Each node of Riak has an ins[tance] of Bitcask running
